analysis.one_liner: Allows Americans to import 90-day supplies of prescription drugs from approved Canadian pharmacies.
analysis.headline: The bipartisan bill, led by a Republican committee chairman and 13 cosponsors, never received a hearing or vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require the FDA, within 180 days, to write rules letting individuals buy prescription drugs from certified Canadian pharmacies and import up to a 90-day personal supply. Purchases would need a valid US prescription, and the drugs would have to match an FDA-approved drug in active ingredients, dose form, and strength. Controlled substances, biologics, and several other categories would be excluded, and the FDA would publish a list of approved pharmacies. Americans who buy the same medicines far more expensively at home would be able to buy them at Canadian prices.
analysis.who_benefits: Americans who pay US prices for prescription drugs, especially people paying cash or with high deductibles, who could buy the same medicines at Canadian prices. Canadian pharmacies certified under the program would also gain customers.

how_it_helps.text: Requires the FDA to issue regulations within 180 days permitting individuals to import prescription drugs purchased from approved Canadian pharmacies for personal use, up to a 90-day supply [S2] [S3].

Limits eligibility to drugs with the same active ingredients, route of administration, dosage form, and strength as FDA-approved drugs, and requires a valid US prescription, to keep the program to genuine equivalents of US medicines [S2] [S3].

Establishes a certification process for Canadian pharmacies — including at least five years in operation, Canadian licensing, quality-assurance and product-testing requirements — and requires the FDA to publish a public list of approved pharmacies so consumers know where it is legal to buy [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug makers, whose US prices would face competition from cheaper Canadian sales of the same medicines, and possibly US retail pharmacies that lose some cash-paying customers. Taxpayers pay nothing directly; the FDA absorbs the cost of writing and enforcing the rules.

drawbacks.text: The program is narrow: it excludes controlled substances, biologics, infused and intravenous drugs, refrigerated drugs, and products made through biotechnology processes, which means it would not touch many of the most expensive medicines, including most new specialty and cancer drugs [S3].

It applies only to personal importation of a 90-day supply, not to bulk or commercial importation, so the savings reach individuals who navigate the program rather than lowering prices across the insurance system.

Critics of drug importation generally argue the FDA cannot fully verify the safety of medicines sourced abroad; the bill addresses this with pharmacy certification and product testing, but a regulator would still be overseeing a foreign supply chain.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For people who pay list prices — the uninsured and those with high deductibles — the savings could be substantial, and the safety provisions are unusually detailed for an importation bill. The main honest objection is scope: because it excludes biologics and other high-cost categories and covers only personal purchases, it would not lower prices for most insured patients, and pharma's loss is limited to the cash-pay market.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never held a hearing or vote on it before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Introduced on January 9, 2019 by Senator Grassley together with Senator Klobuchar [S1] [S3].
Read twice and referred to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions the same day; that referral is the last action in the bill's history [S5].
It drew 12 cosponsors: 10 Democrats, 1 Independent, and 1 Republican [S4].
No further action — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — occurred before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug makers are better off: their US prices never faced Canadian competition, because the committee with jurisdiction never moved the bill despite bipartisan sponsorship.

against.name: Brand-name pharmaceutical industry
against.role: Manufacturers of patented prescription drugs sold at higher US prices

sides.party_line_note: The sponsorship was bipartisan — 12 cosponsors split 10 Democrats, 1 Independent, and 1 Republican behind a Republican lead sponsor — but the Republican-controlled committee of referral never took the bill up.

industries.note: Importation would let Americans buy the same patented medicines at Canadian prices, cutting into the higher prices US patients pay. The industry opposed importation measures throughout this Congress, and the bill never advanced.
Pharmacies certified under the program would gain a new stream of American customers buying 90-day supplies at Canadian prices.

US pharmacies would lose some cash-paying customers to Canadian sellers, though the program's 90-day personal-use limit would keep most prescriptions — especially insured ones — in the domestic system.
